stemMd: Okafor further claims that in 2025 a trip beginning in a district with protected lanes was more likely to end outside that district than a trip beginning in a district without them. Which choice best describes data from the table that support this claim?

options.label: A
options.textMd: In 2025, 41% of trips beginning in Harbour Row and 36% of those beginning in Millgate ended in another district, compared with 22% in Fenwick and 19% in South Quay.

options.label: B
options.textMd: The share of trips ending in another district was highest in Harbour Row, which also had the largest increase in trips since 2023.

options.label: C
options.textMd: About 947 of the trips beginning in Harbour Row in 2025 ended in another district, more such trips than in any other district.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Harbour Row and Millgate together recorded 3,965 weekday trips in 2025, more than Fenwick and South Quay recorded together.

explanationMd:
The claim is about a *likelihood* — how likely a single trip is to end elsewhere. Likelihood is a rate, so the supporting data must be rates, and they must cover both groups.

The table's last column is exactly that rate. Lane districts: 41% and 36%. No-lane districts: 22% and 19%. The lowest lane figure (36%) is still well above the highest no-lane figure (22%), so the claim holds for every pairing. Choice A is the only option built from those rates.

The trap here is Choice D, which is arithmetically correct: $0.41 \times 2{,}310 \approx 947$, and that is more cross-district trips than Millgate's $0.36 \times 1{,}655 \approx 596$. But a count of trips is not a probability per trip. Harbour Row has more cross-district trips partly because it has more trips of every kind.

Check the difference this way: if Fenwick doubled in size overnight with its 22% unchanged, its *count* of cross-district trips could overtake Millgate's while a single Fenwick trip stayed less likely to leave the district. Counts move with size; rates do not.

distractorRationale.d: This compares total trip volume, not the chance that a trip leaves its district. A busier pair of districts could easily have the lower cross-district share, so this figure cannot support the claim.
distractorRationale.b: This reports the top district only, and pairs it with a fact about growth that the claim does not mention. One district's rate cannot establish a difference between two groups of districts.
distractorRationale.c: This converts a rate into a count, which reintroduces district size. The roughly 947 trips follow from 41% of 2,310; a district with more trips overall can lead on the count while a single trip there is no more likely to end elsewhere.

accessibilityText: Using the table of Alderport weekday bicycle-share trips, choose the description of the data that best supports the claim that in 2025 a trip beginning in a district with protected lanes was more likely to end outside that district than a trip beginning in a district without them.

provenance.notes: Original item. All four options are true readings of the table; the item turns on the rate-versus-count distinction.

review.author: digital-sat-wave3-author

independentSolve.workingNotes: The claim is about likelihood, i.e. the share column: 41% and 36% for the lane districts versus 22% and 19% for the others, which is exactly option a.

review.notes: Author solved and checked uniqueness: the claim is about a per-trip likelihood, so only the percentage column supports it, and only A reports that column for both groups. Counts in option D verified: 0.41 x 2310 = 947.1, 0.36 x 1655 = 595.8, 0.22 x 1340 = 294.8, 0.19 x 1455 = 276.5. Awaiting a blind independent solve before publication. Options were reordered after review to remove answer-position bias; ids and labels were remapped with the key.
